findings.evidence: Page 132: "Read off the sample, the long tail looks like this: p50 ≈ 0.80 s, p90 ≈ 0.94 s, p95 ≈ 0.99 s, and p99 ≈ 1.33 s." Page 134, Fig 6.2 labels: 'p50 0.80', 'p90 0.94', 'p95 0.99', 'p99 = 1.33 s', 'mean = 0.85s', 'sample p99 (interpolation) = 1.33s', 'population p99 = 5.0 s'. Page 132 also: "The two-point analytic mean is 0.842 s ... The plotted synthetic stream's exact mean is 0.85 s".
findings.issue: The figure's own caption (p. 134) says the sample p99 of 1.33 s 'is contingent on exactly 100 stragglers in this draw — with 101 of 10,000 the interpolated sample p99 is 5.0 s'. A percentile that flips by a factor of 3.8 on a single-sample change, sitting on a SLO boundary, is the chapter's headline illustration. The chapter does disclose this, but the figure's visual annotation 'p99 = 1.33 s' is rendered as the headline value with the knife-edge caveat only in the caption's reproducibility paragraph, and the figure additionally prints 'population p99 = 5.0 s' as a separate label — so the figure carries two mutually contradictory p99 values as co-equal labels with no visual hierarchy indicating which one the SLO should be judged against. The text (p. 132) adds that 'even this sample's p99 (≈1.33 s) still looks healthy' while the population p99 of 5.0 s sits above the 2 s SLO.
findings.fix_instruction: In Fig 6.2, visually subordinate or re-label the two p99 values so it is unambiguous which is the SLO-relevant one (e.g. 'sample p99 (draw-dependent: 1.33 s at 100 stragglers, 5.0 s at 101)'), and align the figure's caption with the text's own statement that the population p99 (5.0 s) is the SLO-relevant value.

findings.evidence: Page 133: "Concretely: suppose we enable larger dynamic batching to raise raw tokens/s from 50 tok/s to 70 tok/s, but the batch window pushes p95 TTFT from 1.8 s to 2.3 s — above the 2 s SLO. Scenario A [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]: the extra 20 tok/s are produced, but they land in the tail that misses the SLO, so goodput does not grow — goodput is unchanged only at f ≈ 68.6 % (48 ÷ 70)" and: "Scope note: the 50→70 tok/s figures are low-batch decode operating points (Ch 5's illustrative basis, ~14–20 ms/token across the 50–70 tok/s range; canonical batch-1 is 40 tok/s at 25 ms/token)".
findings.issue: Check the arithmetic: 48 ÷ 70 = 68.57% ✓; 50 × 0.96 = 48 ✓; 70 × 0.94 = 65.8 ✓; 70 × 0.65 = 45.5 ✓. The logic is correct and the three scenarios are properly qualified. The defect is the register: the chapter presents this as the worked 'Goodput vs Raw Throughput' example, and the p95 breach (1.8 → 2.3 s) is the trigger — but the canonical p95 TTFT SLO is ≤ 2 s (p. 84), so both 1.8 s and 2.3 s straddle the same 2 s line the chapter elsewhere uses; that is fine. The real issue is that the 50 tok/s baseline used here is the Ch. 5 ILLUSTRATIVE single-stream rate, while the 70 tok/s target is presented as a 'larger dynamic batching' outcome — i.e. an illustrative input is being compared against a batched outcome without a batched baseline, so the 'throughput increase' and the 'compliant fraction' are drawn from different operating points. The scope note acknowledges the rate range but does not resolve the baseline mismatch.
findings.fix_instruction: State in Scenario A that the 50 tok/s baseline is the Ch. 5 single-stream illustrative point while 70 tok/s represents a batched configuration, so the two are not like-for-like, and either supply a batched-to-batched pair or label the comparison explicitly as cross-register.

findings.evidence: Page 141: "the peak demands ~18.6× one host's prefill capacity (18.6 host-equivalents); prefix caching is a partial mitigation (~13% of prefill FLOPs — an upper bound, §6.3.4: the cacheable fraction is smaller once the query tokens are excluded), not the fix. ... at 21 hosts the 344 in-flight peak requests fit the 21 × 17 = 357 resident slots, and the peak prefill oversubscription falls from 18.6× to 51.6 ÷ (21 × 2.77) ≈ 0.9×".
findings.issue: 51.6 ÷ (21 × 2.77) = 51.6/58.17 = 0.887 ≈ 0.9× ✓. The arithmetic checks. The defect is the ~13% prefix-cache figure: p. 138 derives it as 'the byte-identical share is at most the fixed system/instruction portion of the ~1,200-token prompt ... so ~13% of prefill FLOPs (the whole-slot case) is an upper bound on the cacheable fraction' — 1,200/9,200 = 13.04% ✓. But the mini-case then uses ~13% as the mitigation quantity to compute the residual demand: 'it still leaves ~44.9 PFLOP/s of demand against ~2.77 PFLOP/s of sustained capacity, ~16.2 host-equivalents'. Check: 51.6 × (1 − 0.13) = 44.93 ✓ and 44.9/2.77 = 16.2 ✓. The arithmetic is right, but the 13% is an upper bound on the cacheable fraction — the residual computed from an upper bound is therefore an upper bound on the residual, and at 21 hosts the true residual could be lower or higher than 0.9× depending on the actual hit rate. The mini-case presents '0.9×' as the post-fix oversubscription fact without the bound's direction attached.
findings.fix_instruction: State the residual as a bound (≤0.9× on the ~13% upper-bound assumption, ≥0.9× if the cacheable fraction is smaller), and mark the ~16.2 host-equivalents residual as bound-derived rather than measured.

findings.evidence: Page 137: "With the canonical 9.2K KV re-read included, intensity saturates at ~6.8 FLOP/byte (164.1 GFLOP — 140 projection + 24.1 attention — ÷ 24.1 GB of canonical 9.2K FP16 KV; ~5.8 at batch 32), so decode stays bandwidth-bound at every batch size — Ch 8."
findings.issue: Three problems in one sentence. (a) '24.1 attention' GFLOP is not a FLOP count: the decode attention work against a 9.2K cache is ~19.3 TFLOP (2×2×L×d_model×n_layers as above) — the number 24.1 is the KV cache's byte count in GB, i.e. a unit slip between bytes and FLOPs. (b) The stated conclusion 'decode stays bandwidth-bound at every batch size' is contradicted by the corrected arithmetic: with 19.3 TFLOP of attention FLOPs against 24.1 GB of KV, the attention portion alone runs at ~800 FLOP/byte, far above the ~295 ridge, so the KV-attention portion is compute-bound, not bandwidth-bound — and the book states the opposite on p. 50 ('the attention portion reads KV cache at an intensity of only ~1 FLOP/byte for the full-MHA canonical model ... and stays bandwidth-bound at every realistic batch size'). (c) The '~1 FLOP/byte' figure on p. 50 is likewise wrong for the same reason: decode attention per token is ~19.3 TFLOP against 24.1 GB, i.e. ~800 FLOP/byte, not ~1.
findings.fix_instruction: Recompute the decode attention intensity from the model's own geometry (2·2·L·d_model·n_layers FLOPs against 2·n_layers·L·d_model bytes) — which simplifies to 2 FLOP/byte for full dense attention, ~16 FLOP/byte for GQA-8 — and correct the ~1, ~6.8 and ~5.8 FLOP/byte figures in Ch. 6 §6.3.3 and Ch. 2 §2.3 accordingly, including the 'stays bandwidth-bound at every batch size' conclusion.

findings.evidence: Page 129: "1. Workload metrics — what the system is being asked to do. Requests per second (rps) and the token profile (input length, output length, context length). These are the independent variables — the offered load; we do not control them, we characterize them. Admitted concurrency is a serving/scheduler state (Little's law), not a workload input. Fig 6.1's workload box lists concurrency alongside rps and the token profile: read that entry as offered concurrency — the arrival-side λ that the traffic offers — not as admitted or queued concurrency, which sits on the serving/scheduler side with queue depth."
findings.issue: The chapter reads 'Admitted concurrency is a serving/scheduler state (Little's law)' and then instructs the reader to read Fig 6.1's 'concurrency' entry as *offered* concurrency. But Ch. 4 (pp. 84, 96) is emphatic that request concurrency is a Little's-law-derived quantity (Lexec = λ × Wexec ≈ 86 / 344) and that 'concurrent users' is the population measure — there is no 'offered concurrency' quantity anywhere in the canonical scenario. Ch. 4 §4.6 (p. 106) even says 'Requests in flight ≠ KV-resident sequences'. So Ch. 6 introduces a third concurrency concept ('offered concurrency, the arrival-side λ') that does not exist in the book's canonical vocabulary, and describes concurrency as 'the arrival-side λ' — which is a rate, not a concurrency.
findings.fix_instruction: Remove 'offered concurrency' from Fig 6.1's workload box (or rename it 'request rate / arrival pattern'), and align Ch. 6's classification with Ch. 4's: population (active users) → arrival rate (λ) → in-flight requests (λ·W) → resident KV slots, with the note that concurrency is a derived serving-side quantity.

findings.evidence: Page 132: "Under the canonical p95 TTFT SLO of ≤ 2 s, even this sample's p99 (≈ 1.33 s) still looks healthy — the population p99 is 5.0 s, sitting on the straggler cluster." Page 134 Fig 6.2 annotation: 'SLO 2 s (TTFT budget)' — the figure labels the 2 s line as the 'TTFT budget'.
findings.issue: Ch. 4 (p. 84) and the Preface distinguish 'TTFT SLO 1.2 s (retrieval ~120 ms + prefill); p95 ≤ 2 s' — i.e. 1.2 s is the budget and 2 s is the p95 ceiling. The figure's axis label 'SLO 2 s (TTFT budget)' calls the 2 s ceiling the 'budget', which contradicts the canonical ledger's terminology and makes the 1.2 s budget invisible in the figure. This is the same terminology collision as P1-070, but in the figure's own annotation.
findings.fix_instruction: Relabel Fig 6.2's line as 'p95 TTFT ceiling: 2 s' (and, if the figure permits, add the 1.2 s design budget as a second, distinct line), so the figure's annotation matches Table 4-2's terminology.

findings.chapter: 6 — Measuring What Matters: From Telemetry to Architecture Decisions
findings.evidence: 'With the canonical 9.2K KV re-read included, intensity saturates at ~6.8 FLOP/byte (164.1 GFLOP — 140 projection + 24.1 attention — ÷ 24.1 GB of canonical 9.2K FP16 KV; ~5.8 at batch 32), so decode stays bandwidth-bound at every batch size — Ch 8.'
findings.issue: The denominator is not the same at the two displayed operating points. 164.1 ÷ 24.1 = 6.8 counts both the projection and attention FLOPs but divides by KV bytes only, silently dropping the 140 GB weight read that appears in the same sentence's numerator. The quoted ~5.8 at batch 32 is obtained only if weight bytes are included: 32 × 164.1 = 5251.2 GFLOP ÷ (32 × 24.1 + 140) = 911.2 GB = 5.76 ≈ 5.8. A consistent batch-1 combined intensity is 164.1 ÷ (140 + 24.1) ≈ 1.0 FLOP/byte, not 6.8. Separately, 'saturates' contradicts the displayed decline from 6.8 to 5.8. The bandwidth-bound conclusion may still hold (both values are far below the ridge ~295), but the displayed arithmetic does not support the stated numbers.
findings.fix_instruction: State one denominator rule and apply it at both points: if weight bytes are counted when weights appear in the numerator, batch 1 is ~1.0 FLOP/byte and batch 32 is ~5.8 FLOP/byte. Remove 'saturates' or show a monotonic curve with its formula, and reconcile the wording with the Ch. 8 roofline treatment.
